To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

individuals who had higher antibodies against the pathogenic oral bacteria Porphyromonas gengivalis had a 2-fold higher risk of pancreatic cancers, and individuals with higher levels of antibodies to specific commensal (not pathogenic) oral bacteria had a 45%-reduction in their risk of developing pancreatic cancers.

high levels of antibodies to Porphyromonas Gingivalis, a periodontal bacteria that causes gum disease, were associated with a higher risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) in a large European cohort study, whereas high levels of antibodies overall to commensal oral (non-pathogenic oral) bacteria were associated with a lower risk of PDAC.

individuals with high levels of plasma antibodies against a specific pathogenic periodontitis-associated bacterium, Porphyromonasgingivalis ATCC 53978, had a twold higher risk of developing pancreatic cancer than individuals who had low levels of antibodies against this bacterium.

oral bacteria might have a role in pancreatic cancer pathogenesis, and that the immune response to oral bacteria might protect against pancreatic cancer.
periodontitis may be a risk factor for pancreatic cancer and that the immune response to oral bacteria may be a marker of the risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
